newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Most Asia stocks end lower, rise in yen hits Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Most Asia stocks end lower, rise in yen hits Tokyo.

text.p: Most Asian stock markets ignored Wall Street's record close and ended lower on Wednesday, with Japanese stocks hurt by a rising yen.

Japan's key 225-share Nikkei index closed down 242.62 points, or 1.18 percent, at 20,289.93 on Wednesday on the yen's strength. A strong yen hurts Japanese exports by making them more expensive overseas. The U.S. currency dropped below 111 yen, its lowest level since November 20, 1996, following a warning by U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers that Japan should avoid running up external trade surpluses.
The warning came after news of a more than 90 percent rise in Japan's politically sensitive current account surplus.
On Tuesday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average zoomed past the 7,500 level to end up 60.77 points at 7,539.27 -- the third straight record finish for blue chip stocks.
But Asian markets generally ignored Wall Street's cheer.
In Hong Kong, stocks ended a roller-coaster session down 18.19 points, or 0.13 percent, at 14,421.52.
"Rumours and bad news on properties, red chips and H-shares expedited the pace of the price fall," said Peter Lui of NAVA SC Securities.
He said the market was hurt by possible government measures to cool speculation in the property market and Beijing's recent drive to curb speculative trading in Chinese stock markets.

After the close, U.S. brokerage Merrill Lynch said it expected a 10 to 15 percent correction in Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index from recent highs and that it would reduce its weighting in Hong Kong in favour of South Korea and the Philippines.

Philippine stocks tacked on modest gains, bolstered by the advance in the Dow and the Supreme Court's decision to reject a petition that sought to change the Constitution to allow President Ramos a second term.
The main index ended 12.63 points, or 0.46 percent, higher at 2,787.74.
Elsewhere in Asia, Thai stocks were hit following the central bank's latest moves to prevent foreigners from repatriating baht funds obtained through stock trading.
The SET index was off 5.82 points, or 1.10 percent, at 521.40.

Taiwan stocks turned lower after opening mixed as profit-taking dragged down the electronics sector, considered a bellwether for the market. The index finished down 125.98 points, or 1.50 percent, at 8,267.00.
Indonesian shares erased earlier losses and closed higher on a late wave of selected blue-chip buying. The composite Index was up 3.27 points, or 0.47 percent, at 693.04.
Korean stocks ended lower as large-cap stocks underwent a correction. The composite index fell 4.04 points to 765.79.

Malaysian stocks were dragged down by selling in Telekom Malaysia, which lost 30 cents to 12.20 ringgit. The company announced earlier this week it was buying a 20.12 percent stake in a Thai telecommunications firm.
The Composite index ended down 2.11 points, or 0.19 percent, at 1,108.25.
Singapore's Straits Times Index closed off 21.29 points, or 1.06 percent, at 1,993.49 and Australia's All Ordinaries Index lost 15.2 points, or 0.58 percent, to close at 2,613.7.
In New Zealand, a sharp gain in Telecom and a solid improvement in the forestry sector hoisted the New Zealand share market. It closed 17.42 points higher at 2,384.97.
